decisions.quote: The present high-powered and pre-registered study seeks to contribute to research on cognitive effects of masculine generics by replicating and extending one particular study, namely, a roughly 20-years old study on the effects of masculine generics in German speakers (Stahlberg et al., 2001, Study 2; Stahlberg & Sczesny, 2001, Study 3, is the same study).
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state that they are replicating one particular study and that Stahlberg & Sczesny (2001, Study 3) is the same study as Stahlberg et al. (2001, Study 2), making this blind target a duplicate of the original study already recorded in row 2002 rather than an omitted independent target.

decisions.quote: That is, for both the experimental condition that produced the lowest inclusion of women (i.e., masculine generics) and the highest inclusion of women (capital-I), the number of women listed by participants in the present study and by participants two decades ago did not differ statistically. Although not a true experimental test, this convergence in absolute numbers indicates that the changes regarding the visibility and increased power of women in society did not lead to an overall increased cognitive accessibility of women. Only for masculine-feminine word pairs, our results differed from the original study. In our replication, significantly more women were listed in this condition than in the masculine generics condition, whereas this contrast was not significant in the original study.
decisions.reason: Evaluating the hierarchy of statements across the full source shows that the outcome is mixed rather than successful. First, the pairwise contrast between masculine-feminine word pairs and masculine generics is a core tested finding of the original 3x2 design that the authors explicitly highlighted in the Introduction (p. 2, lines 108-125) and powered their study to test (p. 5, lines 420-422). Second, in Results (p. 8, lines 897-902), the statement 'Taken together, our results replicate those found by Stahlberg et al. (2001)' is immediately scoped by 'In particular, (1)... (2)... (3)... (4)...' to the four ANOVA-level patterns (the omnibus effect of linguistic expression, the relative ordering where capital-I exceeds word pairs, the main effect of participant gender, and the null interaction); it does not cover the simple contrast of word pairs versus masculine generics, and the immediately following paragraph (lines 903-915) shows that the word-pair condition mean differed significantly from the original study. Third, when synthesizing the replication as a whole in the opening paragraph of the Discussion (pp. 9-10, lines 1111-1154), the authors themselves qualify the convergence as holding for the pattern of main effects and for 2 of the 3 original conditions (masculine generics and capital-I), while explicitly marking the third condition as a deviation: 'Only for masculine-feminine word pairs, our results differed from the original study. In our replication, significantly more women were listed in this condition than in the masculine generics condition, whereas this contrast was not significant in the original study.' Under the codebook, finding an effect where the original found none is a disagreement (not merely a stronger effect size), and when a paper confirms the focal effect it set out to test while explicitly marking another tested finding as differing from the original in its own words, the summary of focal/main effects does not override the stated contrast and the outcome must be coded as mixed.

decisions.quote: Taken together, our results replicate those found by Stahlberg et al. (2001). In particular, (1) the linguistic expression of gender affected the extent to which women were listed by participants, with masculine generics leading to the lowest percentage of women listed; (2) this effect was more pronounced for the capital-I and for the gender asterisks conditions (the latter was not included in the original study) than for the feminine-masculine word-pair condition; (3) there was a large effect of participant gender (female participants listed more women than did male participants); and (4) the two factors did not interact.
decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall verdict that their results replicate Stahlberg et al. (2001), which under Rule 1 decides the outcome as successful and outweighs the individual contrast noted for the masculine-feminine word-pair condition (attributed by the authors to higher statistical power in the replication).
